name: Quakers
summary: Quakers (the Religious Society of Friends) are a Christian movement founded in mid-17th-century England around the Inner Light, the direct guidance of God in every person, without creed or clergy. Their testimonies of peace, equality, integrity (including refusing oaths), simplicity and community lead them to reject war and all use of weapons, capital punishment and compulsion in religion, and to campaign against slavery and for prison reform. The sources record no stated position on most economic, constitutional and cultural questions.
scope: The historic Quaker tradition as Britannica and the New World Encyclopedia define it: the testimonies (peace, equality, integrity, simplicity, community) and the texts they tie to it: Barclay's Apology, Penn's Brief Account, and the corporate statements in Britain Yearly Meeting's book of discipline. Branches differ (Britannica names Evangelical, Pastoral, Liberal and Conservative Friends), so questions on which branches split (such as same-sex marriage or abortion, where Friends have no united view) are null. The individual voices in the book of discipline are not taken as the movement's position unless presented as a testimony or as a yearly-meeting statement.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: The Advices ask Friends to show loving consideration for all creatures and to use power over nature with reverence for life.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Barclay says that killing, banishing, fining or imprisoning anyone for his conscience or difference in worship or opinion proceeds from the spirit of Cain.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Friends oppose all use of weapons and coercion by force, and every preparation for war, which includes arming fighters abroad.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Quakers historically reject a formal or salaried clergy and have no central governing authority; Penn describes refusing compelled maintenance of a national ministry.

clerical-rule.rationale: Barclay holds Christ's kingdom is not of this world and the gospel is extrinsic to the rule and government of political states; Quakers also reject a distinct clergy.

collective-defense.rationale: Friends oppose all military alliances and all use of weapons, so an armed response owed to an ally's attack contradicts the testimony.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Simplicity is a testimony: the Advices say to resist the desire to acquire possessions and not to buy what you do not need, and Brinton calls shunning superfluities of possessions the heart of Quaker ethics.

death-penalty.rationale: Britain Yearly Meeting declares its unwavering opposition to capital punishment, and the book of discipline names protest against it as a fruit of the testimony to the sacredness of life.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Britannica records Quaker spiritual equality of the sexes and active support for women's suffrage, and the book of discipline counts the emancipation of women among causes Quaker action helped.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: A Quaker statement on the United Nations rejects on principle the provisions for coercion in its charter, while supporting its work of negotiation.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: A yearly-meeting statement printed in the book of discipline totally opposes all military alliances.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Barclay says justice is to be administered upon all without respect of persons, and Friends hold all people equal in the eyes of God and deserving equal treatment.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Friends oppose all wars and all use of force by arms, which rules out war to keep a region in a state.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Britain Yearly Meeting declared that no one has the right to use hydrogen bombs in his defence, and Friends oppose all preparation for war and all weapons.

initiating-nondefensive-force-unjustifie.rationale: Quakers reject all war and weapons, defensive included ('war or fight in any Case'), so they hold that no use of force is justified, initiating it outside defence included.

military-force-for-human-rights.rationale: A Quaker yearly-meeting statement opposes all wars and all use of weapons and coercion by force, 'no end could ever justify such means', and Barclay forbids war in any case.

military-superiority.rationale: The Advices ask whether Friends maintain the testimony that war and the preparation for war are inconsistent with the spirit of Christ, and a yearly meeting opposes all preparation for war.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Barclay says those with fullness are to be willing to help the need of those allotted less, and the Quaker advice on income is that the good of others and the community should guide how Friends use it.

people-in-arms.rationale: Quakers oppose bearing arms and all use of weapons in any case, so replacing a professional army with an armed citizenry contradicts their testimony.

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: Barclay holds it unlawful for Christians 'to war or fight in any Case' and the Advices call war and the preparation for war inconsistent with the spirit of Christ; the peace testimony is the best known Quaker testimony.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Woolman, quoted in the book of discipline, says possessions are equitable only while faithfully improved to the good of the whole, and no possession acquired or inherited justifies using others for luxury.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Britannica records that Quakers were among the earliest to oppose slavery, joined the American civil rights movement and opposed the apartheid regime.

rehabilitation.rationale: A Quaker statement emphasises redemptive treatment rather than retributive punishment and holds that imprisonment should be a means of reforming criminals.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Barclay condemns fining or imprisoning anyone for the exercise of conscience, and Quakers were persecuted for refusing oaths, tithes and military service and won affirmation instead of oaths.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Barclay claims for people of peaceable conversation the liberty to worship and to admit those their persuasion convinces, 'without being therefore molested by the Civil Magistrate'.

separate-church-state.rationale: Barclay denies the magistrate any jurisdiction over conscience and worship, and Penn records that Quakers refuse tithes or compelled maintenance for a national ministry as unlawful.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Barclay holds that the magistrate has no power over conscience or worship and that the gospel is extrinsic to the government of political states.

notes: Themes searched: peace and war, oaths and honesty, state and religion, equality, prisons and punishment, simplicity and property, environment, economy, family and sexuality, government. Texts read: Barclay's Apology (Propositions X, XIV, XV), Penn's Brief Account, Britain Yearly Meeting's Quaker faith & practice chapters 1, 3, 5, 11, 20, 22-25 and 27, Britannica and New World Encyclopedia. Economy, constitutional design, immigration and trade were searched in the book of discipline and found only as individual voices or organisational projects, which are not taken as the movement's position. Fox's autobiography was read for the founder's account but supplies no separate answer.
